question: How do you detect a cycle in a linked list? Explain the time and space complexity.
answer: I would use Floyd's tortoise and hare. One pointer moves one node at a time and the other moves two. If there is a cycle, the fast pointer eventually meets the slow pointer inside the loop; if the fast pointer reaches null, the list has no cycle. It runs in O(n) time because the fast pointer closes the gap by one node per step, and it uses O(1) extra space, unlike a hash set of visited nodes, which needs O(n) memory. To find where the cycle starts, I reset one pointer to the head and move both one step at a time until they meet.

question: Explain the difference between an array and a linked list. When would you use each?
answer: An array stores elements next to each other in memory so you can get any element by its index quickly. A linked list stores nodes that point to the next node. I would use an array when I need fast access by index and a linked list when I insert and delete a lot.

question: What causes a React component to re-render?
answer: React re-renders when something changes. It is the virtual DOM that makes it fast. Usually you should use useMemo everywhere to stop re-renders.

question: What are React keys, and why do stable keys matter?
answer: Keys tell React which list item is which between renders, so it can match old and new elements during reconciliation. If I use a stable ID from the data, React keeps each item's state and DOM node attached to the right element when the list is reordered or filtered. If I use the array index and an item is inserted at the top, every index shifts, so React may reuse the wrong component: an input can keep the text that belonged to another row. Keys only need to be unique among siblings, not globally.

question: How would you protect your API from excessive requests?
answer: I would add rate limiting, for example with express-rate-limit, so each IP can only make a certain number of requests per minute. If we run several servers, the counters should be stored in Redis so the limit is shared. I would also return 429 with a Retry-After header.

question: How would you make a payment or order endpoint idempotent when clients retry?

question: How does a compound index work, and why does the order of its fields matter?
answer: A compound index sorts entries by the first field, then by the second within each value of the first, and so on. That is why it supports queries that filter on a prefix of the fields: an index on (userId, createdAt) serves 'all orders for a user, newest first' efficiently, but not a query on createdAt alone, because those values are scattered across users. I usually put equality filters first, then the sort field, then range filters. The trade-off is extra storage and slower writes, so I only add indexes that real queries use.

question: Tell me about a disagreement with a teammate and how you handled it.
answer: In my final-year project, a teammate wanted to rewrite our Express backend in Django two weeks before the demo, because he found the Express code messy. I asked for a short call and listed what we would lose: the auth and payment routes we had already tested. I suggested a middle path: I would refactor the two messiest route files that week, and we would note Django as future work in the report. He agreed after seeing the refactored files. We demoed on time, and the examiner praised the clean structure. I learned to answer a frustration with a concrete small change instead of arguing about the whole plan.

question: Tell me about a decision you made with incomplete information. How did it turn out?
answer: As the lead for our college placement portal, I had to choose between building our own login or using Google sign-in, with no data on how many students had college Google accounts. The IT office estimated roughly 70% did, so I chose Google sign-in plus an email fallback, and set a rule to revisit after the first drive. After launch, 85% of students used Google sign-in and support tickets about passwords dropped to almost zero. The fallback mattered for the rest. In hindsight I should have asked for an exact count earlier; it took one email.
